rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window and avoid missing late compounds. This should show whether peaks are compressed early, late, or spread across the gradient so later runs can trim phi and adjust slope.

All 10 compounds eluted cleanly and well before the end, so trim the gradient window to the observed elution region to reduce run time while keeping similar slope and all peaks inside the gradient. This tests whether a narrower, better-centered window can preserve full resolution with a lower time penalty.

The first method already had perfect resolution term, so the main opportunity is to cut time. A shorter gradient at the same phi window and temperature will test how much compression the critical mid-cluster can tolerate while reducing the run-time penalty.

The 10 min run is very fast but over-compresses the central cluster, especially peaks 6 and 7. Increasing only tG should show whether that critical pair is slope-sensitive and recover enough resolution while likely keeping the time term at or near zero.

The critical pair clearly improves with shallower slope, and 14 min is already near optimal with no time penalty. A small increase to 16 min should test whether the 6/7 pair crosses the key resolution threshold while still keeping the run comfortably short.

The 6/7 pair is the only persistent limitation, and its moderate response to tG suggests temperature may shift selectivity enough to improve it without sacrificing the short run. Testing a 5 C decrease at the current best slope probes whether that pair is temperature-sensitive.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing peaks 5 and 6, so probe the opposite direction at the best 14 min gradient. A 5 C increase may improve the critical central selectivity enough to beat the current best without adding time penalty.

Temperature changes hurt, so keep 40 C and bracket the optimum slope more finely between 10 and 14 min. A 12 min gradient will test whether the maximum CRF sits just below 14 min, potentially with a better resolution-time tradeoff.

The central cluster is strongly slope-sensitive and resolution continues improving from 14 to 16 min; testing 18 min checks whether extra spread gives a further CRF gain despite some time penalty. This helps define whether 14 min was truly optimal or just the best point sampled so far.

The broad 0.05–0.95 window likely wastes organic range after the last peak; slightly lowering phi1 while keeping the best tG may trim the effective gradient and alter central selectivity enough to improve the 6/7 pair without increasing run time. This is a targeted phi-window test after slope and temperature mapping.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved CRF, so continue tightening the upper end of the gradient window around the actual elution region. This may further improve central selectivity while all peaks should still remain comfortably within the gradient.

The 0.05–0.90 window improved over 0.95, but 14 min may be slightly longer than needed for maximum CRF. Testing the same optimized phi window at 12 min checks whether a modestly steeper gradient preserves enough central resolution to reach or exceed the current best with even less run time.

With the improved 0.90 upper limit, a slightly shallower slope than the current best may lift the 6/7 pair above the apparent scoring threshold while keeping only a small time penalty. This directly tests whether the best CRF is at the same phi window but 2 minutes longer.

The upper window optimization helped, so now test whether slightly raising phi0 trims unused low-organic range without harming early peaks; the first peak is still retained enough that 0.10 should be safe. This may subtly reposition the crowded middle group and improve CRF at the current best tG and T.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved CRF, and the first peak at 1.45 min is still safely retained, so one more step may further center the gradient on the useful elution range. This directly tests whether the crowded mid-cluster benefits from eliminating more unused low-organic time.

The best result came from raising phi0 to 0.10, while lowering phi1 to 0.85 previously gave full resolution but a slight time penalty at phi0 0.05. Combining the better lower bound with the tighter upper bound may keep all peaks within the gradient and improve the central pair enough to push CRF higher.

We have already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000, so the priority is to avoid repeating methods while checking nearby conditions that might also sit on the optimum plateau. Raising phi0 one more step with the current best upper bound tests robustness of the optimum and may reveal another equally maximal setting.

We are on a clear optimum plateau, so continue mapping its edge without repeating successful settings. Increasing phi0 another step checks how far the lower bound can be raised before early retention or the central-pair resolution starts to degrade.

The optimum plateau seems centered near phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.85, so test the lower edge of phi1 while keeping the best lower bound. This explores whether a slightly tighter upper window can still maintain full resolution with zero time penalty or whether 0.85 is already the sweet spot.

Since phi1 0.80 with phi0 0.10 was too low at the upper end, pair it with the other optimal lower bound to map the plateau corner and confirm whether the best region is truly centered at phi1 0.85. This avoids repetition while refining the boundary of the max-CRF zone.

With 12 min too steep and 14 min optimal, use one remaining run to confirm the upper slope boundary around the best phi window. This checks whether the max-CRF plateau extends to 16 min at phi0 0.10 or drops immediately from the optimum.
